2103.11320_table_13.enriched_title: Neutral triple generation performance by category for COMeT variants
2103.11320_table_13.enriched_content: Category-wise neutral triple scores from ConceptNet are compared between COMeT and a mitigation variant (COMeT-Filtered) using the Neutral Mean metric (higher is better). COMeT achieves Neutral Mean values of 55.7 (Origin), 43.5 (Religion), 56.4 (Gender), 57.0 (Profession), and 55.8 (Overall). COMeT-Filtered improves neutrality, reaching 60.2 for Origin and 51.8 for Religion and yielding the best reported Overall Neutral Mean of 60.2, indicating consistent gains over the base model in the shown entries.

2109.03952_formula_1.label: Formula
2109.03952_formula_1.content: $$H = \tanh (E) \quad \alpha = \operatorname {s o f t m a x} \left(w ^ {T} H\right) \quad r = \tanh \left(E \alpha^ {T}\right) \tag {1}$$
2109.03952_formula_1.enriched_title: Tanh encoding, softmax attention weights, and pooled representation

variables.E: input matrix of element/sequence representations (e.g., token embeddings or encoder states)
variables.H: nonlinear transformed representations after applying tanh to E
variables.w: trainable weight vector used to score each representation
variables.alpha: softmax-normalized attention weight vector over elements in E/H
variables.r: final pooled/summary representation computed as an attention-weighted combination

2109.03952_formula_1.enriched_content: The equation defines an attention-style pooling mechanism to summarize a set or sequence of vectors. First, the input representations E are passed through a tanh nonlinearity to produce H, which can stabilize and enrich features. Then a trainable vector w scores each element via w^T H, and softmax converts these scores into attention weights alpha that sum to one. Finally, r is computed as a tanh-transformed weighted combination of E using alpha, yielding a single vector summary emphasized toward the most relevant elements.

2.2 Fairness Attribution with Attention Weights

The aforementioned classification model with the attention mechanism combines input feature embeddings by taking a weighted combination. By manipulating the weights, we can intuitively capture the effects of specific features on the output. To this end, we observe the effect of each attribute on the fairness of outcomes by zeroing out or reducing its attention weights and recording the change. Other works have used similar ideas to understand the effect of attention weights on accuracy and evaluate interpretability of the attention weights by comparing the difference in outcomes in terms of measures such as Jensen-Shannon Divergence (Serrano and Smith 2019) but not for fairness. We are interested in the effect of features on fairness measures. Thus, we measure the difference in fairness of the outcomes based on the desired fairness measure. A large change in fairness measure and a small change in performance of the model would indicate that this feature is mostly responsible for unfairness, and it can be dropped without causing large impacts on performance. The overall framework is shown in Fig. 1. First, the outcomes are recorded with the original attention weights intact (Fig. 1a). Next, attention weights corresponding to a particular feature are zeroed out, and the difference in performance and fairness measures is recorded (Fig. 1b). 2109.03952_figure_1.enriched_title: Attention-weight attribution pipeline for fairness impact estimation
2109.03952_figure_1.enriched_content: Multiple feature embeddings (f1…fm producing e1…em) feed an attention module that outputs an instance representation r, which is then passed through stacked dense layers to produce the baseline prediction out. A parallel branch modifies the attention weights by setting some to zero (or otherwise perturbing them), applies renormalization to obtain a new representation r′, and propagates it through the same dense-layer stack to produce an alternative output out′. The attribution signal is defined by the difference between out and out′, quantifying how specific features’ attention contributions affect the model output in terms of fairness-versus-accuracy changes.

The advantage of our work is that this trade-off curve can be controlled by controlling how many features and by how much to be manipulated which is not the case for most existing work.

Interpretability. In this work, we introduced an attribution framework based on the attention weights that can analyze fairness and accuracy of the models at the same time and reason about the importance of each feature on fairness and accuracy. There is a body of work in NLP literature that tried to analyze the effect of the attention weights on interpretability of the model (Wiegreffe and Pinter 2019; Jain and Wallace 2019; Serrano and Smith 2019). Other work also utilized attention weights to define an attribution score to be able to reason about how transformer models such as BERT work (Hao et al. 2021). Notice that although Jain and Wallace (2019) claim that attention might not be explanation, a body of work has proved otherwise including (Wiegreffe and Pinter 2019) in which authors directly target the work in Jain and Wallace (2019) and analyze in detail the problems associated with this study.
